title: Where the horses were tied outside
summary: The state's horse racing industry generates billions in annual economic impact, provides jobs and preserves open space, writes Alyse Cohen, but it needs help, particularly the off-track betting parlors like the one she operates, that have seen profits plummet.
content:
by Alyse Cohen, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

by Alyse Cohen, Maryland Matters April 13, 2026

My father took me to the Cracked Claw in Frederick, which was a seafood restaurant and also, in the way that Maryland places sometimes doubled as themselves, an off-track betting parlor. You could eat steamed crabs and watch a race happen somewhere else on a screen mounted above the bar.

It sounds improbable. It was completely ordinary. I understood, in the way children understand things before they can name them, that this was how a place held together, not by being one thing cleanly, but by accommodating the full range of what people actually wanted to do on a Tuesday evening.

That was August 1992, the year Gov. William Donald Schaefer legalized off-track betting. I didn’t know it was a big policy moment for Maryland, I only knew it as a place where my father and I sat together and watched horses run.

There is a quality to things that are genuinely local that is difficult to manufacture and easy to lose. It has to do with the way rural businesses and families in the same buildings carry memory. Frederick had that. The farms around it had that. The whole equine ecosystem of central Maryland also had it with the breeders, the farriers, the feed dealers and the trainers.

What has happened since is not a tragedy exactly, but it is a change being discussed in certain ways before our General Assembly this year. Maryland now has 120 racing dates a year where it once had 175. The number of Maryland-bred foals — the next generation of the whole enterprise — has been cut nearly in half in three years. Pimlico, one of the most historic racetracks in the world, sat in rubble long enough that the State Sen. J.B. Jennings (R-Harford and Baltimore) said so plainly at a committee hearing, and no one disputed it.

The off-track betting parlors that were meant to extend the reach of racing have watched revenues fall so far that one operator reported earning $8,000 last year — for the entire year — on a facility the size of a small airplane hangar. He still owes the mortgage. I own an OTB today and it is down 38% in revenue year-over-year. The reason we went before lawmakers was that we’re worried our industry is dying.

There is something that deserves calling out loudly when a local industry is dying. Someone has to draw attention to it, because when businesses close, they do it too quietly. The shuttering doesn’t announce itself. It just goes. The horses are still there, the farms still there, the people who built their lives around this still there, and then one day the math stops working and the thing that was ordinary becomes memory.

In November, Gov. Wes Moore signed an executive order acknowledging what anyone who grew up around horses in this state already knew: the equine sector is not a relic. It generates $2.9 billion in annual economic impact. It employs an entire human ecosystem. It keeps open land open. The order called for a strategic plan, a coordinated future, a recognition that this industry is worth the deliberate effort of saving. The report is due in September 2026.

Senate Bill 639 is a less poetic than the executive order. It would have authorized wagering on historical horse races at licensed OTB facilities, capped at 4,000 terminals, overseen by the Gaming Commission, subject to a public referendum. It have would let the places that have survived — the OTBs, the small betting parlors, the rooms where people still gather to watch races on screens above the bar — compete for some portion of the $40 million in gaming revenue that currently crosses state lines every year because Maryland has given them no alternative product to offer.

Certain gaming businesses oppose it. This is understandable. It is also, when you look at it clearly, an argument that the machinery built to serve one part of Maryland’s life should be allowed to outlast the older life it displaced. I don’t think that’s what anyone intended. I think it is simply what happens when policy moves faster than the places policy is supposed to remember.

I grew up knowing that you could ride a horse to a roadhouse and tie it up outside while you went in and became briefly part of something larger than your own evening. That world is not entirely gone. But it requires, as all living things do, some conditions in which to continue. The legislature was asked to provide some of those conditions. I hope they remember what it felt like to be in a room where the horses were still tied up outside.
